claim: Rod photoreceptors can respond to a single photon and mediate vision in dim light.
source: Rods can respond to a single photon and mediate vision in dim light.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge about rod photoreceptor function in the introduction.

claim: Cone photoreceptors are less sensitive to light than rods and mediate color vision.
source: Cones are less sensitive to light and mediate color vision.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge about cone photoreceptor function in the introduction.

claim: Photoreceptor specialization results from well-defined rod- and cone-specific patterns of gene expression.
source: Photoreceptor specialization results from well-defined rod- and cone-specific patterns of gene expression (Kefalov, 2012; Siegert et al., 2012), which are in part controlled by retinal transcription factors (TFs) OTX2, CRX, NRL, and NR2E3.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: OTX2 determines photoreceptor cell fate in both rods and cones.
source: In both rods and cones, OTX2 determines photoreceptor cell fate (Nishida et al., 2003), and CRX regulates expression of terminal photoreceptor genes (Furukawa et al., 1997).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Nishida et al., 2003.

claim: CRX regulates expression of terminal photoreceptor genes in both rods and cones.
source: In both rods and cones, OTX2 determines photoreceptor cell fate (Nishida et al., 2003), and CRX regulates expression of terminal photoreceptor genes (Furukawa et al., 1997).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Furukawa et al., 1997.

claim: Rod photoreceptor fate and gene activation are induced by NRL and its downstream target NR2E3.
source: Rod photoreceptor fate and gene activation are induced by NRL and its downstream target NR2E3 (Mears et al., 2001).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Mears et al., 2001.

claim: Loss of NR2E3 leads to enhanced S-cone syndrome, an autosomal recessive human retinal disease.
source: Loss of NR2E3 leads to enhanced S-cone syndrome, an autosomal recessive human retinal disease (Haider et al., 2000) that is recapitulated in retinal degeneration 7 (rd7) mice (Haider et al., 2001).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Haider et al., 2000 and 2001.

claim: rd7 rods retain expression of rod-specific genes but also de-repress a subset of cone-specific genes.
source: rd7 rods show a partial conversion of photoreceptor identity because they retain expression of rod-specific genes but also de-repress a subset of cone-specific genes (Chen et al., 2005; Corbo and Cepko, 2005; Peng et al., 2005).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Chen et al., 2005; Corbo and Cepko, 2005; Peng et al., 2005.

claim: Rods make up 70–80% of all mouse retinal cells.
source: Because rods make up 70–80% of all mouse retinal cells and outnumber cones by 35:1 (Jeon et al., 1998), whole retina studies can approximate features of rods but mask differences between rods and cones that contribute to their unique identities.
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Jeon et al., 1998.

claim: Rods outnumber cones by 35:1 in mouse retina.
source: Because rods make up 70–80% of all mouse retinal cells and outnumber cones by 35:1 (Jeon et al., 1998), whole retina studies can approximate features of rods but mask differences between rods and cones that contribute to their unique identities.
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Jeon et al., 1998.

claim: There is a high positive correlation between accessible chromatin and local regions of low DNA methylation in various cell types.
source: Of special interest is the high positive correlation between accessible chromatin and local regions of low DNA methylation that has been observed in various cell types (Stadler et al., 2011; Hon et al., 2013; Ziller et al., 2013; Mo et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to multiple studies.

claim: TF binding can result in local regions of low DNA methylation.
source: TF binding can result in local regions of low DNA methylation, leading to strong overlaps between regions identified as DNA hypo-methylated and as accessible chromatin.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge in the field.

claim: The rod nucleus is approximately 5 μm in size.
source: Also of interest is the small size of the rod nucleus (~5 μm; Solovei et al., 2009) and its highly condensed chromatin (Kizilyaprak et al., 2010), which may potentially impact how chromatin accessibility correlates with DNA methylation.
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Solovei et al., 2009.

claim: Rod nuclei have highly condensed chromatin.
source: Also of interest is the small size of the rod nucleus (~5 μm; Solovei et al., 2009) and its highly condensed chromatin (Kizilyaprak et al., 2010), which may potentially impact how chromatin accessibility correlates with DNA methylation.
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Kizilyaprak et al., 2010.

claim: Rods are the only known cell type in mice with nuclei that have heterochromatin centers surrounded by peripheral euchromatin.
source: In addition, rods are the only known cell type in mice with nuclei that have heterochromatin centers surrounded by peripheral euchromatin (Carter-Dawson and LaVail, 1979).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Carter-Dawson and LaVail, 1979.

claim: The inverted chromatin organization in rods is thought to facilitate nocturnal vision.
source: This inverted organization is thought to facilitate nocturnal vision (Solovei et al., 2009).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Solovei et al., 2009.

claim: Cone nuclei are larger than rod nuclei and exhibit the conventional arrangement of central euchromatin and peripheral heterochromatin.
source: By contrast, cone nuclei are larger and exhibit the conventional arrangement of central euchromatin and peripheral heterochromatin.
evidence: This is stated as a comparison to rod nuclei based on established knowledge.

claim: Most rod-specific regions of low DNA methylation are not located in accessible chromatin in adult rods.
source: Unexpectedly, most rod-specific regions of low DNA methylation are not located in accessible chromatin in adult rods.
evidence: This is a primary finding from the study's data analysis.

claim: Rod-specific hypo-methylated regions that are not in accessible chromatin are potential active regulatory sites in fetal neural tissue.
source: Instead, our evidence suggests that these regions are potential active regulatory sites in fetal neural tissue and, despite loss of active chromatin marks, remain hypo-methylated in adult rods due to the barrier to cytosine methyltransferases posed by chromatin condensation.
evidence: This is an interpretation based on the study's data comparing adult and fetal samples.

claim: Hypo-methylated regions in adult rods remain unmethylated due to the barrier to cytosine methyltransferases posed by chromatin condensation.
source: Instead, our evidence suggests that these regions are potential active regulatory sites in fetal neural tissue and, despite loss of active chromatin marks, remain hypo-methylated in adult rods due to the barrier to cytosine methyltransferases posed by chromatin condensation.
evidence: This is a hypothesis proposed based on the study's findings.

claim: NR2E3 function is necessary for rods to gain their complete ensemble of epigenomic features.
source: Integrated analysis of rd7 rods, together with normal rods and cones, shows that NR2E3 function is necessary for rods to gain their complete ensemble of epigenomic features.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the integrated analysis of rd7 rods compared to normal rods and cones.

claim: 16617 rod and 15888 cone discrete unmethylated regions (UMRs) were identified with median mCG = 6%.
source: Using previously defined criteria (Stadler et al., 2011; Burger et al., 2013), we identified two types of regions that are depleted for DNA methylation: (1) 16617 rod and 15888 cone discrete (<5 kb) un-methylated regions (UMRs; median mCG = 6%), which tend to be at promoters, and (2) 85992 rod and 65791 cone low-methylated regions (LMRs; median mCG = 24%), which are likely associated with distal regulatory regions (Supplementary file 2).
evidence: This is a quantitative result from the MethylC-seq data analysis.

claim: 85992 rod and 65791 cone low-methylated regions (LMRs) were identified with median mCG = 24%.
source: Using previously defined criteria (Stadler et al., 2011; Burger et al., 2013), we identified two types of regions that are depleted for DNA methylation: (1) 16617 rod and 15888 cone discrete (<5 kb) un-methylated regions (UMRs; median mCG = 6%), which tend to be at promoters, and (2) 85992 rod and 65791 cone low-methylated regions (LMRs; median mCG = 24%), which are likely associated with distal regulatory regions (Supplementary file 2).
evidence: This is a quantitative result from the MethylC-seq data analysis.

claim: 55366 regions in rods and 75650 regions in cones with increased ATAC-seq densities mark accessible chromatin.
source: We identified a set of 55366 regions in rods and 75650 regions in cones with increased ATAC-seq densities that mark accessible chromatin (Supplementary file 3).
evidence: This is a quantitative result from the ATAC-seq data analysis.

claim: In both rods and cones, ATAC-seq peaks exhibit low levels of DNA methylation.
source: In both rods and cones, ATAC-seq peaks exhibit low levels of DNA methylation (Figure 1B).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 1B.

claim: Hypo-methylated regions have elevated ATAC-seq signals on average.
source: On average, hypo-methylated regions also have elevated ATAC-seq signals (Figure 1C), and UMRs show strong overlap with ATAC-seq peaks (Figure 1D).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 1C.

claim: UMRs show strong overlap with ATAC-seq peaks.
source: On average, hypo-methylated regions also have elevated ATAC-seq signals (Figure 1C), and UMRs show strong overlap with ATAC-seq peaks (Figure 1D).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 1D.

claim: 38% of cone LMRs overlap with ATAC-seq peaks.
source: 38% (24830) of cone LMRs overlap with ATAC-seq peaks, a percentage close to previous reports in embryonic stem cells and cortical neurons (Xie et al., 2013; Mo et al., 2015).
evidence: This is a quantitative result from the data analysis comparing LMRs and ATAC-seq peaks.

claim: Only 19% of rod LMRs overlap with ATAC-seq peaks.
source: Yet, only 19% (15984) of rod LMRs overlap with ATAC-seq peaks.
evidence: This is a quantitative result from the data analysis comparing LMRs and ATAC-seq peaks.

claim: 31% of rod LMRs show no sign of chromatin accessibility (<0.1 ATAC-seq FPKM).
source: In fact, 31% of rod LMRs show no sign of chromatin accessibility (<0.1 ATAC-seq FPKM), whereas this fraction is only 7% for cones.
evidence: This is a quantitative result from the data analysis.

claim: Only 7% of cone LMRs show no sign of chromatin accessibility (<0.1 ATAC-seq FPKM).
source: In fact, 31% of rod LMRs show no sign of chromatin accessibility (<0.1 ATAC-seq FPKM), whereas this fraction is only 7% for cones.
evidence: This is a quantitative result from the data analysis.

claim: Rods harbor a substantial compartment of demethylated, but inaccessible, DNA that is largely absent in cones.
source: This analysis shows that rods harbor a substantial compartment of demethylated, but inaccessible, DNA that is largely absent in cones.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the comparative analysis of rods and cones.

claim: 49% of cone LMRs overlap Nrl KO ATAC-seq peaks.
source: Similar to our results using purified nuclei, a greater fraction of cone LMRs overlap Nrl KO ATAC-seq peaks (49%; 31952) compared to rod LMRs that overlap WT ATAC-seq peaks (26%; 22590) (Figure 1—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is a quantitative result from the analysis using whole retina samples.

claim: 26% of rod LMRs overlap WT ATAC-seq peaks.
source: Similar to our results using purified nuclei, a greater fraction of cone LMRs overlap Nrl KO ATAC-seq peaks (49%; 31952) compared to rod LMRs that overlap WT ATAC-seq peaks (26%; 22590) (Figure 1—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is a quantitative result from the analysis using whole retina samples.

claim: A subset of active enhancers in embryonic tissue have low levels of DNA methylation in adult tissues in the absence of ongoing enhancer activity.
source: A previous study demonstrated that a subset of active enhancers in embryonic tissue have low levels of DNA methylation in adult tissues in the absence of ongoing enhancer activity (Hon et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Hon et al., 2013.

claim: Vestigial enhancers are hypo-methylated regions that are not enriched for active histone marks and DNaseI hypersensitivity in adult cells.
source: Referred to as vestigial enhancers, these hypo-methylated regions are not enriched for active histone marks and DNaseI hypersensitivity in adult cells.
evidence: This is a definition based on previous literature.

claim: Rod LMRs have a bimodal distribution of <100 bp ATAC-seq signals.
source: When we examine the densities of sub-nucleosomal-length ATAC-seq reads, a subset of reads that may better capture sites of TF binding (He et al., 2014), we observe a bimodal distribution of rod ATAC-seq signals at LMRs (Figure 1E), with the lower peak at nearly zero signal.
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 1E.

claim: The distribution of rod ATAC-seq signals at LMRs is significantly different from that of cone ATAC-seq signals at LMRs (bootstrap Kolmogorov-Smirnov p<2.2 x 10–16).
source: This distribution is significantly different than that of cone ATAC-seq signals at LMRs (bootstrap Kolmogorov-Smirnov p<2.2 x 10–16) and potentially reflects a greater number of vestigial enhancers in rod, compared to cone, LMRs.
evidence: This is a statistical result from the data analysis.

claim: There are more DMRs with lower methylation levels in rods than in cones (10784 rod hypo-DMRs versus 6693 cone hypo-DMRs).
source: We find a greater number of DMRs that have lower methylation levels (hypo-DMRs) in rods than in cones (10784 rod hypo-DMRs versus 6693 cone hypo-DMRs).
evidence: This is a quantitative result from the DMR analysis.

claim: DNA methylation levels at DMRs around gene transcription start sites show a strong negative correlation with gene expression, with a trough Pearson correlation of -0.8 4 kb downstream of the TSS.
source: As expected from previous studies (Schultz et al., 2015), DNA methylation levels at DMRs around gene transcription start sites (TSSs) show a strong negative correlation with gene expression, with a trough Pearson correlation of -0.8 4 kb downstream of the TSS (Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1 and is consistent with previous studies.

claim: Only 3% of rod hypo-DMRs overlap rod ATAC-seq peaks.
source: Similar to our results using LMRs, we find that rod hypo-DMRs are especially discordant with accessible chromatin: only 307 (3%) of rod hypo-DMRs overlap rod ATAC-seq peaks, compared with 1475 (22%) of cone hypo-DMRs that overlap cone ATAC-seq peaks (Figure 2B).
evidence: This is a quantitative result from the data analysis.

claim: 22% of cone hypo-DMRs overlap cone ATAC-seq peaks.
source: Similar to our results using LMRs, we find that rod hypo-DMRs are especially discordant with accessible chromatin: only 307 (3%) of rod hypo-DMRs overlap rod ATAC-seq peaks, compared with 1475 (22%) of cone hypo-DMRs that overlap cone ATAC-seq peaks (Figure 2B).
evidence: This is a quantitative result from the data analysis.

claim: The large majority of rod hypo-DMRs are depleted for ATAC-seq signal.
source: In rods the large majority of hypo-DMRs are depleted for ATAC-seq signal (Figures 2C–D), active histone modifications H3K4me1 and H3K27ac (Figure 2E), and retinal photoreceptor TF binding (Figure 2F), and they are located distally from promoters (Figure 2G; Figure 2—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figures 2C-D.

claim: The large majority of rod hypo-DMRs are depleted for active histone modifications H3K4me1 and H3K27ac.
source: In rods the large majority of hypo-DMRs are depleted for ATAC-seq signal (Figures 2C–D), active histone modifications H3K4me1 and H3K27ac (Figure 2E), and retinal photoreceptor TF binding (Figure 2F), and they are located distally from promoters (Figure 2G; Figure 2—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 2E.

claim: The large majority of rod hypo-DMRs are depleted for retinal photoreceptor TF binding.
source: In rods the large majority of hypo-DMRs are depleted for ATAC-seq signal (Figures 2C–D), active histone modifications H3K4me1 and H3K27ac (Figure 2E), and retinal photoreceptor TF binding (Figure 2F), and they are located distally from promoters (Figure 2G; Figure 2—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 2F.

claim: Rod hypo-DMRs are located distally from promoters.
source: In rods the large majority of hypo-DMRs are depleted for ATAC-seq signal (Figures 2C–D), active histone modifications H3K4me1 and H3K27ac (Figure 2E), and retinal photoreceptor TF binding (Figure 2F), and they are located distally from promoters (Figure 2G; Figure 2—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 2G and Figure 2—figure supplement 2.

claim: Most rod hypo-DMRs have low levels of DNA methylation in fetal cortex.
source: Supporting the idea that rod hypo-DMRs may be enriched for enhancers that function earlier in neural development, most rod hypo-DMRs have low levels of DNA methylation in fetal cortex (Figure 2C,H) and are enriched for active histone modifications in fetal brain (Figure 2E).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figures 2C and 2H.

claim: Most rod hypo-DMRs are enriched for active histone modifications in fetal brain.
source: Supporting the idea that rod hypo-DMRs may be enriched for enhancers that function earlier in neural development, most rod hypo-DMRs have low levels of DNA methylation in fetal cortex (Figure 2C,H) and are enriched for active histone modifications in fetal brain (Figure 2E).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 2E.

claim: Disruption of NR2E3 in rd7 rods preserves the inverted chromatin arrangement but reduces chromatin condensation.
source: To address this question, we took advantage of the observation that disruption of NR2E3 in rd7 rods preserves the inverted chromatin arrangement, but reduces chromatin condensation (Corbo and Cepko, 2005).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Corbo and Cepko, 2005.

claim: rd7 rods are hypo-methylated at rod hypo-DMRs but show higher methylation levels than WT rods.
source: We find that whereas rd7 rods are also hypo-methylated at rod hypo-DMRs, including those that may encompass vestigial enhancers, they show higher methylation levels than WT rods (Figure 2C,H).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figures 2C and 2H.

claim: Chromatin condensation plays a role in limiting the methylation of vestigial enhancers.
source: Taken together, these data are consistent with a role for chromatin condensation in limiting the methylation of vestigial enhancers.
evidence: This is an interpretation based on the comparative data from WT and rd7 rods.

claim: 22520 ATAC-seq peaks show >2-fold increased accessibility in Nrl KO retina.
source: In comparing WT and Nrl KO retinas, 22520 ATAC-seq peaks show >2-fold increased accessibility in Nrl KO retina, but only about a third as many (7916 peaks) have greater accessibility in WT retina (Figure 3A).
evidence: This is a quantitative result from the differential ATAC-seq analysis.

claim: 7916 ATAC-seq peaks show >2-fold increased accessibility in WT retina.
source: In comparing WT and Nrl KO retinas, 22520 ATAC-seq peaks show >2-fold increased accessibility in Nrl KO retina, but only about a third as many (7916 peaks) have greater accessibility in WT retina (Figure 3A).
evidence: This is a quantitative result from the differential ATAC-seq analysis.

claim: WT-enriched regions of accessible chromatin cluster near the promoters of rod-specific genes.
source: WT-enriched regions of accessible chromatin cluster near the promoters of rod-specific genes (Supplementary file 5) and have high levels of H3K27ac, H3K4me1, and H3K4me3 (Figure 3B–D).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figures 3B-D and Supplementary file 5.

claim: WT-enriched accessible chromatin regions have high levels of H3K27ac, H3K4me1, and H3K4me3.
source: WT-enriched regions of accessible chromatin cluster near the promoters of rod-specific genes (Supplementary file 5) and have high levels of H3K27ac, H3K4me1, and H3K4me3 (Figure 3B–D).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figures 3B-D.

claim: Nrl KO-enriched accessible chromatin cluster near promoters of cone-specific genes.
source: In contrast, Nrl KO-enriched accessible chromatin cluster near promoters of cone-specific genes (Figure 3B,C).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figures 3B and 3C.

claim: A higher percentage of NRL binding sites overlap WT-enriched ATAC-seq peaks rather than Nrl KO-enriched peaks.
source: A higher percentage of binding sites for NRL and CRX in WT retina overlap WT-enriched, rather than Nrl KO-enriched, peaks (Figure 3E).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 3E.

claim: A higher percentage of CRX binding sites in WT retina overlap WT-enriched ATAC-seq peaks rather than Nrl KO-enriched peaks.
source: A higher percentage of binding sites for NRL and CRX in WT retina overlap WT-enriched, rather than Nrl KO-enriched, peaks (Figure 3E).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 3E.

claim: CRX binding sites in Nrl KO retina show higher overlap with Nrl KO-enriched peaks.
source: However, CRX binding sites in Nrl KO retina show higher overlap with Nrl KO-enriched peaks.
evidence: This is a result from the analysis of CRX ChIP-seq data in Nrl KO retina.

claim: One previously identified enhancer near Nr2e3 induced reporter activity in WT but not in Nrl KO retinas.
source: Within the sensitivity limits of the assay, one previously identified enhancer near Nr2e3 (Hsiau et al., 2007) induced reporter activity in WT but not in Nrl KO retinas (Figure 4, top), and four out of five regions near cone-specific genes induced reporter activity in Nrl KO but not in WT retinas (Figure 4, bottom; Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4.

claim: Four out of five regions near cone-specific genes induced reporter activity in Nrl KO but not in WT retinas.
source: Within the sensitivity limits of the assay, one previously identified enhancer near Nr2e3 (Hsiau et al., 2007) induced reporter activity in WT but not in Nrl KO retinas (Figure 4, top), and four out of five regions near cone-specific genes induced reporter activity in Nrl KO but not in WT retinas (Figure 4, bottom; Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4 and Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: The majority (5/6) of regions that had detectable reporter expression showed cell type-specificity.
source: Although the electroporation experiments tested only a limited number of regions, the majority (5/6) of regions that had detectable reporter expression showed cell type-specificity.
evidence: This is a summary of the electroporation experiment results.

claim: A motif matching the canonical CRX motif is enriched in all three peak sets (WT-specific, Nrl KO-specific, and shared) relative to random sequences.
source: Consistent with CRX binding data (Figure 5—figure supplement 1B), a motif matching the canonical CRX motif (p<1 x 10–10; Gupta et al., 2007) is enriched in all three peak sets (WT-specific, Nrl KO-specific, and shared) relative to random sequences (Figure 5A, left) and is the top motif for both Nrl KO retina and shared peaks.
evidence: This is supported by motif analysis data shown in Figure 5A.

claim: A motif matching CTCF shows the second strongest enrichment in shared peaks against random sequences.
source: A motif matching CTCF (p<1 x 10–5) shows the second strongest enrichment in shared peaks against random sequences (Figure 5A, middle).
evidence: This is supported by motif analysis data shown in Figure 5A.

claim: 87% of ATAC-seq peaks with the strongest (top 20%) CTCF binding sites show DNaseI hypersensitivity in >30% of mouse tissues surveyed by ENCODE.
source: Shared peaks with the strongest CTCF binding sites appear to be located in accessible chromatin in a broad range of cell types: 87% of ATAC-seq peaks with the strongest (top 20%) CTCF binding sites show DNaseI hypersensitivity in >30% of mouse tissues surveyed by ENCODE (Stamatoyannopoulos et al., 2012), compared to only 35% of peaks in the remainder (bottom 80%) that lack strong CTCF binding sites.
evidence: This is a result from comparing CTCF binding sites with ENCODE DNaseI hypersensitivity data.

claim: Only 35% of ATAC-seq peaks in the bottom 80% that lack strong CTCF binding sites show DNaseI hypersensitivity in >30% of mouse tissues surveyed by ENCODE.
source: Shared peaks with the strongest CTCF binding sites appear to be located in accessible chromatin in a broad range of cell types: 87% of ATAC-seq peaks with the strongest (top 20%) CTCF binding sites show DNaseI hypersensitivity in >30% of mouse tissues surveyed by ENCODE (Stamatoyannopoulos et al., 2012), compared to only 35% of peaks in the remainder (bottom 80%) that lack strong CTCF binding sites.
evidence: This is a result from comparing CTCF binding sites with ENCODE DNaseI hypersensitivity data.

claim: Gkm-SVM can distinguish Nrl KO-specific regions from random regions based on regulatory sequences with auROC = 0.91.
source: Although the WT-specific set was too small for the gkm-SVM analysis, the Nrl KO-specific (auROC = 0.91) and shared (auROC = 0.86) regions can be distinguished from random regions based on regulatory sequences contained within the peaks (Figure 5B,C).
evidence: This is a result from the gkm-SVM analysis shown in Figures 5B and 5C.

claim: Gkm-SVM can distinguish shared regions from random regions based on regulatory sequences with auROC = 0.86.
source: Although the WT-specific set was too small for the gkm-SVM analysis, the Nrl KO-specific (auROC = 0.91) and shared (auROC = 0.86) regions can be distinguished from random regions based on regulatory sequences contained within the peaks (Figure 5B,C).
evidence: This is a result from the gkm-SVM analysis shown in Figures 5B and 5C.

claim: Gkm-SVM trained on WT retina ATAC-seq could predict retinal enhancer activity as assessed by a massively parallel reporter assay.
source: Further supporting the ability of our gkm-SVM model to predict enhancer activity, we find that a gkm-SVM trained on WT retina ATAC-seq could predict retinal enhancer activity as assessed by a massively parallel reporter assay (Shen et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by analysis of data from Shen et al., 2016.

claim: The Pearson correlation between the gkm-SVM WT retina ATAC-seq score and the average retinal CRE expression level is 0.427 (p<10–320).
source: Among the 12858 constructs with RNA detected in at least one replicate, the Pearson correlation between the gkm-SVM WT retina ATAC-seq score and the average retinal CRE expression level is 0.427 (p<10–320).
evidence: This is a statistical result from the analysis of the massively parallel reporter assay data.

claim: Candidate CREs that score in the top 10% of gkm-SVM scores are 4-fold enriched for high-level expression.
source: Relative to all candidate CREs, those that score in the top 10% of gkm-SVM scores are 4-fold enriched for high-level expression (Figure 5—figure supplement 2B).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 2B.

claim: Pearson correlations of ATAC-seq signal between rd7 and WT retina is r = 0.91.
source: Pearson correlations of ATAC-seq signal between rd7 and WT retina (r = 0.91; Figure 6A) and between rd7 and Nrl KO retina (r = 0.88; Figure 6B) are both higher than the correlation between WT and Nrl KO retina (r = 0.78; Figure 3C).
evidence: This is a statistical result from the ATAC-seq data analysis shown in Figure 6A.

claim: Pearson correlations of ATAC-seq signal between rd7 and Nrl KO retina is r = 0.88.
source: Pearson correlations of ATAC-seq signal between rd7 and WT retina (r = 0.91; Figure 6A) and between rd7 and Nrl KO retina (r = 0.88; Figure 6B) are both higher than the correlation between WT and Nrl KO retina (r = 0.78; Figure 3C).
evidence: This is a statistical result from the ATAC-seq data analysis shown in Figure 6B.

claim: The rd7 rod chromatin shows a hybrid rod/cone phenotype.
source: These correlations indicate that the rd7 rod chromatin shows a hybrid rod/cone phenotype, recapitulating previous observations from gene expression studies (Chen et al., 2005; Corbo and Cepko, 2005; Peng et al., 2005).
evidence: This is an interpretation based on the correlation data and is consistent with previous studies.

claim: 44 ATAC-seq peaks within 10 kb of rod-specific genes show greater than two-fold higher signal in WT retina compared to rd7 retina.
source: Notably, 44 ATAC-seq peaks within 10 kb of rod-specific genes show greater than two-fold higher signal in WT retina compared to rd7 retina, whereas only one peak displays the opposite pattern.
evidence: This is a quantitative result from the differential ATAC-seq analysis.

claim: Peaks near cone genes that are normally repressed in rods by NR2E3 show higher chromatin accessibility in rd7 retina compared to WT retina.
source: Reciprocally, peaks near cone genes that are normally repressed in rods by NR2E3 (e.g., Gnat2, Pde6c, Pde6h, Gnb3) show higher chromatin accessibility in rd7 retina compared to WT retina.
evidence: This is a result from the ATAC-seq data analysis.

claim: Very few regions show differences in DNA methylation between rd7 rods and WT rods: 287 regions are hypo-DMRs in rd7 rods and 1385 regions are hypo-DMRs in WT rods.
source: With respect to their DNA methylation, very few regions show differences between rd7 rods and WT rods: 287 regions are hypo-DMRs in rd7 rods and 1385 regions are hypo-DMRs in WT rods.
evidence: This is a quantitative result from the DMR analysis.

claim: A comparison of rd7 rod versus cone methylomes reveals 1981 regions that are hypo-DMRs in rd7 rods and 4929 regions that are hypo-DMRs in cones.
source: A comparison of rd7 rod versus cone methylomes reveals more differences: 1981 regions are hypo-DMRs in rd7 rods and 4929 regions are hypo-DMRs in cones.
evidence: This is a quantitative result from the DMR analysis.

claim: Intragenic and promoter levels of DNA methylation are lower in rods at rod-specific genes and in cones at cone-specific genes.
source: Consistent with previous studies in the retina at targeted genes (Merbs et al., 2012) or using enrichment-based methylation assays (Oliver et al., 2013), intragenic and promoter levels of DNA methylation are lower in rods at rod-specific genes and in cones at cone-specific genes (Figure 6C).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 6C and is consistent with previous studies.

claim: At rod-specific genes, rd7 rod methylation levels generally resemble those seen in WT rods or lie midway between WT rods and cones.
source: At rod-specific genes (e.g., Nrl, Esrrb, Cnga1), rd7 rod methylation levels generally resemble those seen in WT rods or lie midway between WT rods and cones (Figure 6C,D; Figure 6—figure supplement 1–2).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figures 6C, 6D, and Figure 6—figure supplements 1-2.

claim: Both rd7 rods and cones have low Aqp1 RNA abundance and high DNA methylation at the Aqp1 gene, whereas this gene is expressed and de-methylated in WT rods.
source: A rare exception to this pattern occurs at Aqp1 (Figure 6D), a gene coding for an aquaporin water channel (Papadopoulos and Verkman, 2013). Both rd7 rods and cones have low Aqp1 RNA abundance and high DNA methylation at the Aqp1 gene, whereas this gene is expressed and de-methylated in WT rods.
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 6D.

claim: In rd7 rods, most cone-specific genes are methylated, except those that are de-repressed as a result of NR2E3 loss.
source: In rd7 rods, most cone-specific genes are methylated, except those that are de-repressed as a result of NR2E3 loss (Figure 6C,E; Figure 6—figure supplement 1,3).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figures 6C, 6E, and Figure 6—figure supplements 1 and 3.

claim: 782, 635, and 816 long (≥5 kb) UMRs were categorized as DMVs in WT rods, rd7 rods, and cones, respectively.
source: We categorized 782, 635, and 816 long (≥5 kb) UMRs as DMVs in WT rods, rd7 rods, and cones, respectively.
evidence: This is a quantitative result from the DMV analysis.

claim: 89–90% of DMVs are located within 2.5 kb of the TSS.
source: The large majority of these regions are located within 2.5 kb of the TSS (89–90%) and overlap at least one gene body (93–94%).
evidence: This is a quantitative result from the DMV analysis.

claim: 93–94% of DMVs overlap at least one gene body.
source: The large majority of these regions are located within 2.5 kb of the TSS (89–90%) and overlap at least one gene body (93–94%).
evidence: This is a quantitative result from the DMV analysis.

claim: DMV-associated genes are highly enriched for DNA-binding factors.
source: DMV-associated genes are also, consistent with previous studies (Xie et al., 2013; Mo et al., 2015), highly enriched for DNA-binding factors (Figure 7—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is supported by GO analysis shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 1A and is consistent with previous studies.

claim: About half of the merged DMVs (508) show equal or higher methylation in cones (mean mCG = 12.0%) than in WT rods (6.7%), with rd7 rods showing an intermediate methylation level (9.9%).
source: About half of the merged DMVs (508) show equal or higher methylation in cones (mean mCG = 12.0%) than in WT rods (6.7%), with rd7 rods showing an intermediate methylation level (9.9%) (Figure 7—figure supplement 1C, left).
evidence: This is a quantitative result from the DMV analysis shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 1C.

claim: ONECUT1 is an early cone marker that drives cone genesis, acts upstream of NRL, and becomes silenced during cone maturation.
source: Interestingly, ONECUT1 is an early cone marker that drives cone genesis, acts upstream of NRL, and becomes silenced during cone maturation (Emerson et al., 2013; Sapkota et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Emerson et al., 2013 and Sapkota et al., 2014.

claim: Onecut1 overlaps a merged DMV that is 37% methylated in cones, 10% methylated in rods, and 20% methylated in rd7 rods.
source: Onecut1 overlaps a merged DMV that is 37% methylated in cones, 10% methylated in rods, and 20% methylated in rd7 rods.
evidence: This is a quantitative result from the DMV analysis.

claim: The remaining 488 DMVs have higher mCG in WT rods than in cones; the mean methylation level is slightly higher in rd7 rods (14.7%) than in WT rods (13.5%).
source: The remaining 488 DMVs have higher mCG in WT rods than in cones; here, the mean methylation level is slightly higher in rd7 rods (14.7%) than in WT rods (13.5%) (Figure 7—figure supplement 1C, right), which could potentially reflect a non-specific, genome-wide increase in DNA methylation in rd7 rods (see Figure 8A–C).
evidence: This is a quantitative result from the DMV analysis shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 1C.

claim: Epigenomic patterns in rd7 rods generally resemble WT rods, but may not attain the full magnitudes of rod chromatin accessibility or DNA hypo-methylation.
source: In summary, epigenomic patterns in rd7 rods generally resemble those of WT rods, but may not attain the full magnitudes of rod chromatin accessibility or DNA hypo-methylation.
evidence: This is a summary interpretation of the rd7 rod data.

claim: rd7 rods do not match the epigenomic patterns of cones.
source: At the same time, rd7 rods also do not match the epigenomic patterns of cones.
evidence: This is a summary interpretation of the rd7 rod data.

claim: Rods and cones have similar levels of mCG but up to 29- and 7-fold lower levels of mCH, respectively, compared to cerebral cortical neurons.
source: Compared to cerebral cortical neurons (Mo et al., 2015), rods and cones have similar levels of mCG but up to 29- and 7-fold lower levels of mCH, respectively (Figure 8A–C).
evidence: This is a quantitative result from the methylation analysis shown in Figures 8A-C.

claim: Rods and cones have higher mCH levels compared to most other non-brain tissue types (<0.05% mCH).
source: However, rods and cones have higher mCH levels compared to most other non-brain tissue types (<0.05% mCH; Schultz et al., 2015).
evidence: This is a comparison based on data from Schultz et al., 2015.

claim: WT rods have lower mCH (0.11–0.13%) compared to cones (0.42–0.45%).
source: WT rods have lower mCH (0.11–0.13%) compared to cones (0.42–0.45%), whereas rd7 rods show an intermediate mCH level (0.21–0.25%).
evidence: This is a quantitative result from the methylation analysis.

claim: rd7 rods show an intermediate mCH level (0.21–0.25%).
source: WT rods have lower mCH (0.11–0.13%) compared to cones (0.42–0.45%), whereas rd7 rods show an intermediate mCH level (0.21–0.25%).
evidence: This is a quantitative result from the methylation analysis.

claim: mCH accumulates post-mitotically in photoreceptors.
source: Because NR2E3 is expressed after terminal mitoses in rods, our data also suggests that mCH accumulates post-mitotically in photoreceptors, as it does in the brain.
evidence: This is an inference based on the timing of NR2E3 expression and the mCH levels in rd7 rods.

claim: Retinal photoreceptors cluster separately from cortical neurons based on DNA methylation patterns.
source: Hierarchical clustering shows that retinal photoreceptors are tightly clustered, whereas cortical neurons cluster separately.
evidence: This is a result from the hierarchical clustering analysis of DNA methylation data.

claim: Cortical neurons show greater epigenomic distance between neuron subtypes compared to the rod-cone distance.
source: In addition, cortical neurons show greater epigenomic distance between neuron subtypes compared to the rod-cone distance.
evidence: This is a result from the epigenomic distance analysis.

claim: The fetal cortex clusters more closely to mature retinal photoreceptors than to mature cortical neurons based on DNA methylation patterns.
source: Based on their DNA methylation patterns, the fetal cortex clusters more closely to mature retinal photoreceptors than to mature cortical neurons (Figure 8D).
evidence: This is a result from the hierarchical clustering analysis shown in Figure 8D.

claim: Twice as many regions show hypo-methylation only in retinal photoreceptors (63384) compared to those that show hypo-methylation only in cortical neurons (31483).
source: We therefore defined DMRs across all retinal and cortical samples and found twice as many regions that showed hypo-methylation only in retinal photoreceptors (63384) compared to those that showed hypo-methylation only in cortical neurons (31483; Figure 8—figure supplement 2, Supplementary file 4).
evidence: This is a quantitative result from the DMR analysis shown in Figure 8—figure supplement 2.

claim: A larger proportion of retinal hypo-DMRs, compared to cortical hypo-DMRs, display low-to-moderate levels of DNA methylation in fetal cortex.
source: Also consistent with our interpretation, a larger proportion of retinal hypo-DMRs, compared to cortical hypo-DMRs, display low-to-moderate levels of DNA methylation in fetal cortex (Figure 8E).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 8E.

claim: Increased chromatin condensation in rods could potentially pose a barrier to DNA methylation by limiting the accessibility of DNA methyltransferases.
source: Mouse rod nuclei are exceptionally small, and increased chromatin condensation in rods could potentially pose a barrier to DNA methylation by limiting the accessibility of DNA methyltransferases.
evidence: This is a hypothesis proposed to explain the observed data.

claim: rd7 rods have slightly increased nuclear size and lower levels of chromatin condensation compared to rods.
source: In support of this hypothesis, we find that rd7 rods, a hybrid rod/cone cell with slightly increased nuclear size and lower levels of chromatin condensation compared to rods (Corbo and Cepko, 2005), show higher levels of DNA methylation at putative rod vestigial enhancers.
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Corbo and Cepko, 2005.

claim: Dense heterochromatin regions surrounding immunoglobulins or olfactory receptor clusters in brain neurons coincide with regions of low mCH.
source: A previous study showed that dense heterochromatin regions surrounding immunoglobulins or olfactory receptor clusters in brain neurons coincide with regions of low mCH (Lister et al., 2013), consistent with the idea that the highly condensed chromatin in rods could be a global limiting factor to mCH accumulation.
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Lister et al., 2013.

claim: High chromatin compaction could provide a unifying explanation of some of the unique epigenomic features of rod photoreceptors.
source: Taken together, our results suggest that high chromatin compaction could provide a unifying explanation of some of the unique epigenomic features of rod photoreceptors.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the integrated analysis of the data.

claim: Cells in the oligodendrocyte lineage undergo chromatin compaction as they progress from progenitors to mature myelinating oligodendrocytes.
source: For example, cells in the oligodendrocyte lineage undergo chromatin compaction as they progress from progenitors to mature myelinating oligodendrocytes (Shen et al., 2005).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Shen et al., 2005.

claim: A progressive restriction of the accessible chromatin landscape is a hallmark of differentiating cells.
source: A progressive restriction of the accessible chromatin landscape is a hallmark of differentiating cells and can be conceptualized with a genome-centric version of the Waddington landscape of cell differentiation (Waddington, 1940; Stergachis et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Waddington, 1940 and Stergachis et al., 2013.

claim: Rods show fewer accessible chromatin regions than cones, suggesting that a rod could represent a more developmentally restricted cell type than a cone at the epigenomic level.
source: Our finding that rods show fewer accessible chromatin regions than cones suggests that, at the epigenomic level, a rod could represent a more developmentally restricted cell type than a cone.
evidence: This is an interpretation based on the ATAC-seq data.

claim: NRL, perhaps in combination with NR2E3, is necessary to direct photoreceptor precursors to turn off the default S-cone fate and differentiate along the rod lineage.
source: This idea is consistent with current models of photoreceptor genesis, which propose that NRL, perhaps in combination with NR2E3, is necessary to direct photoreceptor precursors to turn off the default S-cone fate and differentiate along the rod lineage (Swaroop et al., 2010).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Swaroop et al., 2010.

claim: rd7 rods fail to attain WT rod levels of chromatin accessibility and DNA hypo-methylation at rod-specific regions.
source: rd7 rods fail to attain WT rod levels of chromatin accessibility and DNA hypo-methylation at rod-specific regions, and they exhibit increased accessibility and hypo-methylation at multiple cone-specific regions.
evidence: This is a summary of the rd7 rod data.

claim: rd7 rods exhibit increased accessibility and hypo-methylation at multiple cone-specific regions.
source: rd7 rods fail to attain WT rod levels of chromatin accessibility and DNA hypo-methylation at rod-specific regions, and they exhibit increased accessibility and hypo-methylation at multiple cone-specific regions.
evidence: This is a summary of the rd7 rod data.

claim: rd7 rods show intermediate patterns of DNA methylation at large hypo-methylated domains that overlap key developmental TF genes.
source: Furthermore, rd7 rods show intermediate patterns of DNA methylation at large hypo-methylated domains that overlap key developmental TF genes.
evidence: This is a summary of the rd7 rod data.

claim: Mapping the epigenomic landscape of rods and cones could be informative for understanding the clinical variability of human retinal diseases.
source: In addition to enriching our understanding of photoreceptor gene regulation, mapping the epigenomic landscape of rods and cones could be informative for understanding the clinical variability of human retinal diseases.
evidence: This is a potential application of the study's findings.

claim: Patients with the same coding region mutation in inherited retinal diseases can differ markedly in the age of onset, rate, and pattern of photoreceptor degeneration.
source: In inherited retinal diseases such as retinitis pigmentosa and Stargardt macular dystrophy, patients with the same coding region mutation can differ markedly in the age of onset, rate, and pattern of photoreceptor degeneration (Shastry, 1994; Fishman et al., 1999; Oh et al., 2004).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Shastry, 1994; Fishman et al., 1999; Oh et al., 2004.

claim: Part of the phenotypic heterogeneity in inherited retinal diseases may be a result of environmental factors such as light exposure.
source: Although part of this phenotypic heterogeneity may be a result of environmental factors such as light exposure (Wright et al., 2010), another contributing factor could be differences in regulatory DNA sequences that would affect the binding of TFs.
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Wright et al., 2010.

claim: Differences in regulatory DNA sequences could be a contributing factor to phenotypic heterogeneity in inherited retinal diseases.
source: Although part of this phenotypic heterogeneity may be a result of environmental factors such as light exposure (Wright et al., 2010), another contributing factor could be differences in regulatory DNA sequences that would affect the binding of TFs.
evidence: This is a hypothesis proposed to explain clinical variability.

claim: Characterizing genome-wide accessible chromatin in rods and cones could identify regions that influence the clinical course of retinal disease.
source: Therefore, characterizing genome-wide accessible chromatin in rods and cones could identify regions that influence the clinical course of retinal disease.
evidence: This is a potential application of the study's findings.

claim: Recent advances in cellular reprogramming have led to the production of stem cell-derived retinal photoreceptors that might be transplanted into the diseased retina to restore vision.
source: Recent advances in cellular reprogramming have led to the production of stem cell-derived retinal photoreceptors that might be transplanted into the diseased retina to restore vision (Lamba et al., 2009; Gonzalez-Cordero et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Lamba et al., 2009 and Gonzalez-Cordero et al., 2013.

claim: The datasets and integrative analyses could help in refining the reprogramming approaches by identifying key regulatory regions that drive photoreceptor identity.
source: Our datasets and integrative analyses could help in refining the reprogramming approaches in current use by identifying key regulatory regions that drive photoreceptor identity, as well as by providing benchmarks for assessing the extent to which the reprogramming process has faithfully recapitulated a normal rod or cone identity.
evidence: This is a potential application of the study's findings.

claim: Lmopc1-Cre; R26-CAG-LSL-Sun1-sfGFP-myc retinas appeared morphologically normal with no retinal degeneration.
source: Lmopc1-Cre; R26-CAG-LSL-Sun1-sfGFP-myc and HRGP-Cre; R26-CAG-LSL-Sun1-sfGFP-myc retinas appeared morphologically normal with no retinal degeneration.
evidence: This is an observation from the experimental mice.

claim: HRGP-Cre; R26-CAG-LSL-Sun1-sfGFP-myc retinas appeared morphologically normal with no retinal degeneration.
source: Lmopc1-Cre; R26-CAG-LSL-Sun1-sfGFP-myc and HRGP-Cre; R26-CAG-LSL-Sun1-sfGFP-myc retinas appeared morphologically normal with no retinal degeneration.
evidence: This is an observation from the experimental mice.

claim: INTACT purification of rod photoreceptors was 97.5% specific (96.7–98.2%; n = 5).
source: Based on fluorescence microscopy of purified nuclei (>400 nuclei/experiment), INTACT purification of rod photoreceptors was 97.5% specific (96.7–98.2%; n = 5), with non-rod nuclei nearly exclusively arising from non-singlet aggregates.
evidence: This is a quantitative result from the INTACT purification validation.
